plain_english: You'll also find endless trouble if you work hard to hide your true feelings and never let anyone see the real you. Many people live fake lives to impress others. But constantly watching yourself becomes torture. You're always afraid someone will catch you acting differently than usual. And we can never relax if we think everyone who looks at us is judging our worth. Many things happen that strip away our disguises, no matter how much we want to keep them on. Even if you succeed at fooling everyone, life is neither happy nor safe when you always have to wear a mask.
original_excerpt: It also proves a fertile source of troubles if you take pains to conceal your feelings and never show yourself to any one undisguised, but, as many men do, live an artificial life, in order to impose upon others: for the constant watching of himself becomes a torment to a man, and he dreads being caught doing something at variance with his usual habits, and, indeed, we never can be at our ease if we imagine that every one who looks at us is weighing our real value: for many things occur which strip people of their disguise, however reluctantly they may part with it, and even if all this trouble about oneself is successful, still life is neither happy nor safe when one always has to wear a mask.

plain_english: But there's real joy in being honest and straightforward. This kind of life is beautiful on its own — it doesn't hide any part of who you are. Yet even this open way of living has some risk. Some people look down on anything they get too close to. But virtue can never become truly contemptible when people see it up close. It's better to be mocked for being simple than to carry the heavy burden of constant pretending.
original_excerpt: But what pleasure there is in that honest straight-forwardness which is its own ornament, and which conceals no part of its character! Yet even this life, which hides nothing from any one runs some risk of being despised; for there are people who disdain whatever they come close to: but there is no danger of virtue's becoming contemptible when she is brought near our eyes, and it is better to be scorned for one's simplicity than to bear the burden of unceasing hypocrisy.

plain_english: Still, we need to be moderate about this. There's a big difference between living simply and living like a slob. We should spend a lot of time alone with ourselves. Being around people who are different from us disrupts everything we've organized. It stirs up emotions that were calm and irritates any weak or half-healed spots in our minds. But we should mix these two things together. We need to alternate between solitude and being around crowds. Solitude will make us miss other people. Crowds will make us miss being alone. Each one balances out the other. Solitude cures us when we're sick of crowds. Crowds cure us when we're sick of solitude.
original_excerpt: Still, we must observe moderation in this matter, for there is a great difference between living simply and living slovenly. Moreover, we ought to retire a great deal into ourselves: for association with persons unlike ourselves upsets all that we had arranged, rouses the passions which were at rest, and rubs into a sore any weak or imperfectly healed place in our minds. Nevertheless we ought to mix up these two things, and to pass our lives alternately in solitude and among throngs of people; for the former will make us long for the society of mankind, the latter for that of ourselves, and the one will counteract the other: solitude will cure us when we are sick of crowds, and crowds will cure us when we are sick of solitude.

plain_english: We shouldn't always keep our minds stretched tight. Sometimes we need to relax with fun activities. Socrates wasn't embarrassed to play with children. Cato would refresh his mind with wine after tiring himself with government business. Scipio would move his victorious warrior's body to music — not with the weak, stumbling steps that are fashionable now, when we sway in our walking with more than feminine weakness. He danced the way men used to dance in the old days during celebrations, with strong, manly movements. He thought there was no shame in being seen this way, even by his enemies. Our minds need to relax. They come back stronger and more energetic after rest. We can't force crops from rich fields forever — constant heavy harvesting will quickly drain their fertility. In the same way, our minds lose their sharpness when we work them without stopping. But they regain their strength after a short period of rest and relief. Non-stop work creates a kind of numbness and dullness.
original_excerpt: Neither ought we always to keep the mind strained to the same pitch, but it ought sometimes to be relaxed by amusement. Socrates did not blush to play with little boys, Cato used to refresh his mind with wine after he had wearied it with application to affairs of state, and Scipio would move his triumphal and soldierly limbs to the sound of music, not with a feeble and halting gait, as is the fashion now-a-days, when we sway in our very walk with more than womanly weakness, but dancing as men were wont in the days of old on sportive and festal occasions, with manly bounds, thinking it no harm to be seen so doing even by their enemies. Men's minds ought to have relaxation: they rise up better and more vigorous after rest. We must not force crops from rich fields, for an unbroken course of heavy crops will soon exhaust their fertility, and so also the liveliness of our minds will be destroyed by unceasing labour, but they will recover their strength after a short period of rest and relief: for continuous toil produces a sort of numbness and sluggishness.

plain_english: People wouldn't want fun and games so much if these activities weren't naturally appealing. But if you indulge in them constantly, they drain all seriousness and strength from your mind. Sleep is necessary to refresh us, but if you sleep for days on end, you'll die. There's a big difference between loosening your grip on something and letting it go completely. The founders of our laws created festivals so people would be encouraged to celebrate in public. They knew we needed to break up our work with entertainment. As I mentioned before, some great men used to give themselves a certain number of holidays each month. Others divided every day into time for play and time for work.
original_excerpt: Men would not be so eager for this, if play and amusement did not possess natural attractions for them, although constant indulgence in them takes away all gravity and all strength from the mind: for sleep, also, is necessary for our refreshment, yet if you prolong it for days and nights together it will become death. There is a great difference between slackening your hold of a thing and letting it go. The founders of our laws appointed festivals, in order that men might be publicly encouraged to be cheerful, and they thought it necessary to vary our labours with amusements, and, as I said before, some great men have been wont to give themselves a certain number of holidays in every month, and some divided every day into play-time and work-time.

plain_english: I remember the great speaker Asinius Pollio had a firm rule: after the tenth hour, he wouldn't handle any business. He wouldn't even read his mail, worried that some new problem might come up. Instead, he used those two hours to shake off all the tiredness he'd built up during the day. Some people take a break in the middle of the day and save lighter work for the afternoon. Our ancestors also had a rule — no new business could be brought up in the Senate after the tenth hour. Soldiers split up their watch duties, and those just back from active duty get to sleep through the entire night without interruption. We need to be kind to our minds and give them rest from time to time. Rest works on the mind like food — it restores our strength.
original_excerpt: Thus, I remember that great orator Asinius Pollio would not attend to any business after the tenth hour: he would not even read letters after that time for fear some new trouble should arise, but in those two hours used to get rid of the weariness which he had contracted during the whole day. Some rest in the middle of the day, and reserve some light occupation for the afternoon. Our ancestors, too, forbade any new motion to be made in the Senate after the tenth hour. Soldiers divide their watches, and those who have just returned from active service are allowed to sleep the whole night undisturbed. We must humour our minds and grant them rest from time to time, which acts upon them like food, and restores their strength.

plain_english: It's also good to take walks outside. Fresh air and a nice breeze lift our spirits and refresh us. Sometimes we get stronger by going for a drive, traveling, changing scenery, or sharing meals with friends and drinking more wine than usual. Sometimes we should even drink until we're drunk — not to drown our sorrows, but just to soak ourselves in wine. Wine washes away our troubles and pulls them up from deep in our minds. It works as medicine for sadness, just like it does for some illnesses. The god who invented wine is called Liber — not because wine loosens our tongues, but because it frees our minds from worry, breaks us out of mental chains, and makes us bolder in everything we try.
original_excerpt: It does good also to take walks out of doors, that our spirits may be raised and refreshed by the open air and fresh breeze: sometimes we gain strength by driving in a carriage, by travel, by change of air, or by social meals and a more generous allowance of wine: at times we ought to drink even to intoxication, not so as to drown, but merely to dip ourselves in wine: for wine washes away troubles and dislodges them from the depths of the mind, and acts as a remedy to sorrow as it does to some diseases. The inventor of wine is called Liber, not from the licence which he gives to our tongues, but because he liberates the mind from the bondage of cares, and emancipates it, animates it, and renders it more daring in all that it attempts.

plain_english: But moderation is healthy in both freedom and wine. People say that Solon and Arcesilaus were heavy drinkers. Critics attack Cato for being a drunk. But anyone who tries to shame him for this will find it easier to turn their attack into praise than to prove Cato ever did anything truly wrong. Still, we shouldn't do this often. We don't want our minds to pick up bad habits. But sometimes we should force ourselves into playfulness and honesty. We should shake off boring seriousness for a while. If we believe the Greek poet, "it is sometimes pleasant to be mad." And Plato always knocked in vain at poetry's door when he was sober. Or if we trust Aristotle, no great genius has ever existed without a touch of madness.
original_excerpt: Yet moderation is wholesome both in freedom and in wine. It is believed that Solon and Arcesilaus used to drink deep. Cato is reproached with drunkenness: but whoever casts this in his teeth will find it easier to turn his reproach into a commendation than to prove that Cato did anything wrong: however, we ought not to do it often, for fear the mind should contract evil habits, though it ought sometimes to be forced into frolic and frankness, and to cast off dull sobriety for a while. If we believe the Greek poet, "it is sometimes pleasant to be mad"; again, Plato always knocked in vain at the door of poetry when he was sober; or, if we trust Aristotle, no great genius has ever been without a touch of insanity.

plain_english: The mind cannot speak with power and beauty unless something stirs it up. It has to reject the ordinary world around it and rise up, filled with sacred fire. Only then can it create something too magnificent for human lips. As long as the mind stays comfortable and safe, it cannot achieve greatness. It must break away from the well-worn path. It must whip itself into a frenzy until it bites the bit and carries its rider to heights that would terrify it if it were climbing alone.
original_excerpt: The mind cannot use lofty language, above that of the common herd, unless it be excited. When it has spurned aside the commonplace environments of custom, and rises sublime, instinct with sacred fire, then alone can it chant a song too grand for mortal lips: as long as it continues to dwell within itself it cannot rise to any pitch of splendour: it must break away from the beaten track, and lash itself to frenzy, till it gnaws the curb and rushes away bearing up its rider to heights whither it would fear to climb when alone.

plain_english: I've told you, my dear Serenus, what can protect peace of mind, what can bring it back when we lose it, and what can stop the vices that secretly eat away at it. But remember this: none of these methods is strong enough to help us keep such a fragile gift unless we guard our wavering mind with intense and constant attention.
original_excerpt: I have now, my beloved Serenus, given you an account of what things can preserve peace of mind, what things can restore it to us, what can arrest the vices which secretly undermine it: yet be assured, that none of these is strong enough to enable us to retain so fleeting a blessing, unless we watch over our vacillating mind with intense and unremitting care.
